name: IDETrace
description: IDETrace is a large-scale behavioral telemetry dataset capturing fine-grained student interactions with an AI-assisted programming environment. The dataset spans 8 classroom deployments across introductory Python courses, comprising 629 students (369 using the AI tutor), 882,367 telemetry events, 15,991 behavioral sequences, 89,015 observable metric observations, and 1,681 labeled queries classified as guided or dependent help-seeking. The dataset supports four benchmark prediction tasks: next behavioral state, error imminence, query imminence, and query type (AI dependency detection).

distribution.name: raw-telemetry
distribution.description: Raw telemetry event streams in JSON format, one file per deployment. Each file contains timestamped IDE events (code edits, terminal runs, errors, AI queries/responses, test results) for all students in that deployment.

distribution.name: behavioral-sequences
distribution.description: Auto-segmented behavioral state sequences in CSV format. Each row is one behavioral segment with state (thinking, implementing, debugging, seekingHelp, testing), thinking subtype, start time, end time, and duration.

distribution.name: window-level-features
distribution.description: Sliding window features (30s window, 5s step) in CSV format. 46 columns including raw telemetry counts, observable metrics, behavioral sequence features, and prediction labels for all four benchmark tasks.

distribution.name: query-level-features
distribution.description: Per-query behavioral features in CSV format. Features computed from the pre-query behavioral window (last AI response to 15 seconds before query). Includes code edit patterns, terminal activity, error handling, timing, and behavioral state durations.

distribution.name: query-labels
distribution.description: Binary query type labels (guided vs dependent) in CSV format. Labels generated by GPT-4o and validated via inter-rater reliability with two human annotators.

dataCollection: Behavioral telemetry was collected from 8 classroom deployments of an AI-assisted Python programming environment during Fall 2024 and Spring 2025 semesters. Students in introductory programming courses used an instrumented web-based IDE that passively recorded all interactions including code edits, terminal commands, errors, AI tutor queries, AI responses, and test results. Data collection was approved under IRB protocol and all students provided informed consent. The AI tutor was integrated into the IDE as an optional chat-based assistant. Three instructors across multiple course sections participated. Tasks included playlist management, grade book operations, and rectangle class implementations, with session durations ranging from 5 minutes to full class periods.
dataCollectionType: Observational study with passive telemetry instrumentation. No experimental manipulation of student behavior.
dataCollectionRawData: Raw telemetry is included in the dataset as JSON event streams. Derived features (behavioral sequences, sliding windows, query-level features) are generated via the included prepare_data.py pipeline.
dataCollectionMissingData: Some students have incomplete sessions due to browser disconnection or early departure. Students who did not use the AI tutor have telemetry but no query-level features. 57 queries were excluded from query-level features due to insufficient pre-query behavioral window (<15 seconds).
personalSensitiveInformation: All data is de-identified with randomized student IDs. No personally identifiable information (names, emails, IP addresses, demographic information) is included. Student code content and AI query/response text are included in raw telemetry but NOT in derived feature files. Query type labels are based on query content but the benchmark prediction task uses only behavioral features.
dataBiases: The dataset reflects introductory CS students at a single US university. It may not generalize to other populations, programming languages, experience levels, or AI tutor implementations. The query type labels were generated by GPT-4o, which shows a conservative bias toward labeling brief but cognitively engaged queries as dependent (Cohen's kappa = .709 vs human raters at .897). This means dependent queries may be slightly over-counted. The distribution of guided vs dependent queries varies across deployments (20-58% guided), reflecting differences in task difficulty, session duration, and instructor scaffolding.
dataUseCases: Research on student-AI interaction in educational settings, behavioral prediction from telemetry data, learning analytics, AI over-reliance and dependency detection, help-seeking behavior analysis, real-time pedagogical intervention systems, and benchmarking ML models on temporal behavioral data.
dataLimitations: Single institution and introductory Python courses only. One AI tutor platform with a specific pedagogical design (Socratic scaffolding approach). Query type taxonomy is binary (guided/dependent) which simplifies the rich spectrum of help-seeking behaviors. Behavioral state segmentation is automated and may contain classification errors. The 15-second anticipation window for query type prediction excludes rapid-fire queries. Small deployment sizes (D4: 14 students, D8: 15 students) limit statistical power for some cross-deployment evaluations.
dataSocialImpact: This dataset supports research aimed at improving AI-assisted education by detecting and potentially mitigating student over-reliance on AI tools. Responsible use of such detection systems should preserve student autonomy and avoid punitive interventions. The behavioral telemetry approach demonstrates that meaningful pedagogical signals can be extracted without invasive monitoring of student content.
dataAnnotationProtocol: Query type labels (guided vs dependent) were generated by GPT-4o using a classification prompt that receives only query content, student code at time of query, and chat history. The prompt operationalizes the executive/instrumental help-seeking distinction (Nelson-Le Gall, 1981). Labels were validated via inter-rater reliability: two authors independently labeled 97 queries achieving Cohen's kappa = .897 (almost perfect agreement). GPT-4o agreement with each human rater was kappa = .709 and .690 (substantial agreement).
dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom web-based labeling interface integrated into the IDE's instructor dashboard. GPT-4o (OpenAI API) for automated classification.
dataAnnotationAnalysis: Inter-rater reliability computed using Cohen's kappa on 97 queries across 25 student sessions. Human-human agreement: 94.8% (kappa = .897). GPT-human agreement: 85.6% and 84.5% (kappa = .709 and .690). GPT shows conservative bias — over-labels brief but cognitively engaged queries as dependent. Five disagreements between human raters were all genuine boundary cases with no systematic bias.
annotatorDemographics: Two graduate student researchers in computer science with expertise in computing education research and human-AI interaction. Both annotators are co-authors of the paper.
